concepts.idea: Committee chairmen, drafting stages and dates are the most swappable facts of this topic.

concepts.rule: At adoption the Constitution had a Preamble, 395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules; it now has 25 Parts and 12 Schedules (about 470 Articles at present). Some provisions are amended by a simple majority outside Article 368; most need a special majority (two-thirds of members present and voting and a majority of total membership of each House); federal matters need in addition ratification by half the States. Article 1 calls India a Union of States, so the federation is not the result of an agreement and no State can secede. The system is parliamentary with a dual executive, collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha and ministers from Parliament; the judiciary is integrated and independent, citizenship is single, and the voting age is 18 (61st Amendment, 1988).

National Emergency is under Article 352, State Emergency under Articles 356 and 365, Financial Emergency under Article 360, all in Part XVIII (Articles 352 to 360). Parts IV-A and XIV-A came with the 42nd Amendment, IX with the 73rd, IX-A with the 74th and IX-B with the 97th; Part VII was repealed by the 7th Amendment. The Schedules run from the First (States and Union Territories) to the Twelfth (Municipalities, 18 matters); the Eighth now has 22 languages, the Ninth came with the First Amendment, the Tenth with the 52nd, the Eleventh (29 matters) and Twelfth with the 73rd and 74th. The Union List has 98, the State List 59 and the Concurrent List 52 subjects at present.

Britain gave parliamentary government, Rule of Law, single citizenship and prerogative writs; the USA gave Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independence of the judiciary and impeachment of the President; Ireland gave the Directive Principles, the method of electing the President and nomination to the Rajya Sabha; Canada a federation with a strong Centre and residuary powers with the Centre; Australia the Concurrent List, freedom of trade and the joint sitting; Weimar Germany the suspension of Fundamental Rights in Emergency; South Africa the amendment procedure; the USSR the Fundamental Duties. The Federal Scheme, the office of Governor, Emergency provisions and advisory jurisdiction come from the Government of India Act, 1935. The Constitution is federal in form and unitary in spirit.
concepts.example: The nomination of twelve members to the Rajya Sabha follows the Irish model, while their election follows the South African model.

concepts.rule: Parliament may change by simple majority, outside Article 368, items such as new States (Articles 2-3), Legislative Councils (169), the Second Schedule, quorum, MPs' pay, citizenship, electoral laws, Union Territories and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules. Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and all other provisions need the special majority; federal provisions (President's election, courts, Seventh Schedule lists, representation of States, Article 368 itself) also need State ratification. Early amendments: 1st Ninth Schedule and Article 19 grounds, 4th Article 31A, 7th 14 States and 6 UTs, 9th Berubari, 11th Vice-President's electoral college, 24th, 25th, 26th privy purses, 31st 545 seats, 36th Sikkim, 38th, 39th, 42nd.

Article 79 makes Parliament the President, the Council of States and the House of the People; it controls the executive (Art 75), amends the Constitution (Art 368) and approves taxes and spending. The Constituent Assembly acted as the Provisional Parliament from 1950 to 1951-52 (Art 379). The Rajya Sabha has at most 250 members (238 from States and UTs, 12 nominated); the present strength is 245 (including 12 nominated), with only Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir represented among UTs. State members are elected by the elected Assembly members by STV. Since 2003 a candidate need be an elector only in some parliamentary constituency. It is never dissolved, a third retires every second year and the term is six years under the RPA 1951; the Vice-President is ex officio Chairman (Art 89(1)).

The Union List has 98 subjects, the Concurrent List 52 and the State List 59 at present, and Parliament can legislate on State List subjects on a Rajya Sabha resolution, in a National Emergency, on request of two or more States, to implement treaties, and during President's Rule. An Ordinance under Article 123 lapses if not approved within six weeks of reassembly. The Executive frames subordinate legislation, watched by the Committee on Subordinate Legislation. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, which shows lack of confidence by rejecting the Motion of Thanks or a Money Bill, or passing a censure, adjournment or cut motion. Parliament amends the Constitution by simple majority, special majority, or special majority with ratification by at least half the States, within the basic structure; only Parliament initiates an amendment.

Committees help Parliament because it has little time and expertise. The Rajya Sabha has at most 250 members (238 elected, 12 nominated), is never dissolved, with one-third retiring every two years, and is elected through proportional representation by single transferable vote; the Lok Sabha (maximum 550, 543 at present) is directly elected by first-past-the-post, and the nomination of Anglo-Indian members ended with the 104th Amendment (2019). A Money Bill is introduced only in the Lok Sabha, the Speaker's decision on its character is final under Article 110(3), and the Rajya Sabha must return it within 14 days; a no-confidence motion lies only in the Lok Sabha. Sessions are summoned by the President with a gap of at most six months.

Petitions, Privileges and Ethics are committees to inquire (15 LS and 10 RS). House-keeping committees: Library (9: 6 + 3), General Purposes, House and the Joint Committee on Salaries and Allowances (15: 10 + 5). The PAC examines appropriation accounts, finance accounts and CAG reports after spending (not demands for grants). The Estimates Committee, the continuous economy committee, suggests economies and the form of estimates and does not examine undertakings allotted to COPU. COPU examines undertakings run on sound business principles. DRSCs cover all ministries (8 under the RS, 16 under the LS). Scrutiny committees check assurances, delegated legislation, papers laid, SC/ST and women welfare, and offices of profit.

Article 124(1) leaves the number of judges to Parliament; the Court began with eight judges and has about 34 now. Judges are appointed by warrant of the President after consultation with judges (the CJI compulsorily); the senior-most judge becomes CJI by convention. A judge must be a citizen and a High Court judge for five years, a High Court advocate for ten years, or a distinguished jurist; there is no minimum age, retirement is at 65 and the oath is taken before the President. S.P. Gupta (1981) held consultation is not concurrence; the Second Judges Case (1993) reversed it; the 1998 Presidential Reference fixed a collegium of the CJI and four senior-most judges.

Article 131 gives exclusive original jurisdiction in Centre-State and inter-State disputes, with exclusions. Article 32 writs are for Fundamental Rights; Articles 132 to 136 give appeals; Article 143 an advisory opinion by a Bench of five or more judges. Article 129 makes it a court of record; contempt is civil or criminal. High Courts began in 1862 at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras; Article 214 gives one per State and the Seventh Amendment allowed common High Courts. There are 25 High Courts, each with its own year of establishment, seat and benches.

Bribery, undue influence, appeals on religion, race, caste or community, false statements and booth capturing are corrupt practices or offences; civil courts are barred and election petitions lie to the High Court with appeal to the Supreme Court. The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) and the Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998) dealt with money power and State funding; the 7.5 per cent corporate cap was lifted in 2017 and the Electoral Bond Scheme (2018) was struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2024. A recognised party candidate needs one proposer and others ten; star campaigner limits are 40 and 20. A national party needs 6 per cent in four states plus 4 seats, or 2 per cent of the Lok Sabha seats (11) from three states, or state-party status in four states; a state party needs one of five conditions (6 per cent plus 2 seats, 6 per cent plus 1 Lok Sabha seat, 3 per cent of seats or 3 seats, 1 seat per 25, or 8 per cent of votes). Further reforms include NOTA (2013), VVPAT and the 2009 security deposits.

The CAG submits reports on appropriation accounts, finance accounts and public undertakings; legal and regulatory audit is obligatory, propriety audit discretionary, and performance audit was clarified in 2006. The Finance Commission (Article 280) has a chairman with public-affairs experience and four members from four listed groups, is constituted afresh every fifth year and makes advisory recommendations on devolution, grants-in-aid and local-body resources; the Sixteenth is chaired by Arvind Panagariya. The UPSC is created by Articles 315-323, its members are appointed by the President, at least half must have ten years' government service, and they hold office for six years or till 65.

The NCBC was set up in 1993 after the Mandal case, became a constitutional body under Article 338B by the 102nd Amendment (2018), and has civil-court powers for inquiry but is investigative and recommendatory, not a court. The Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (Article 350B, 7th Amendment 1956, on the recommendation of the States Reorganisation Commission) is appointed by the President, investigates the safeguards of Articles 29, 30, 347 and 350A and reports to the President; the Constitution does not specify his tenure, qualifications or removal, and his headquarters has been at New Delhi since 2015. Classical-language status needs, among other things, early texts 1500-2000 years old; Tamil (2004), Sanskrit (2005), Telugu and Kannada (2008), Malayalam (2013), Odia (2014) and Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali (2024) have it. The GST Council (Article 279A, 101st Amendment, 2016) is chaired by the Union Finance Minister with the Union Minister of State for Revenue or Finance and one Minister from each State, the Union Revenue Secretary is its ex-officio Secretary and the CBIC Chairperson a non-voting invitee.

concepts.rule: Part III covers Articles 12 to 35 and is called the Magna Carta of India. Originally there were seven rights; the right to property was deleted by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978, leaving six. The rights are not absolute: the State may impose reasonable restrictions, and the courts decide their reasonableness. Parliament can curtail them only by a constitutional amendment, not an ordinary act, and not so as to affect the basic structure. Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended in a National Emergency, and Article 19 is suspended automatically only in an external emergency. The rights are separated into those of citizens only (Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, 30) from those also open to foreigners.

Article 12 includes the Union and state governments and legislatures, local authorities and other authorities such as LIC, ONGC and SAIL. Article 13 voids inconsistent laws and its 'law' covers ordinances, delegated legislation and custom with the force of law. A constitutional amendment is not 'law' under Article 13, but Kesavananda Bharati (1973) allows challenge on the basic structure. Article 14 applies to all persons and permits reasonable classification on an intelligible differentia. Dicey's Rule of Law applies in India in its first two elements. Exceptions include Article 361 immunities, Articles 105 and 194, and Article 31C.

Article 15(1) bars discrimination by the State on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, while 15(2) also binds private persons. Clauses 15(4), 15(5) and 15(6) came by the 1st (1951), 93rd (2005) and 103rd (2019) Amendments. Article 16 adds descent and residence as grounds and allows reservation under 16(4), 16(4A), 16(4B) and 16(6). Indra Sawhney (1992) upheld 27% OBC reservation with the creamy layer excluded, a 50% limit and no reservation in promotions. The 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Amendments responded to parts of that ruling. The creamy-layer ceiling rose from Rs 1 lakh (1993) to Rs 8 lakh (2017).

Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes its enforcement an offence; the 1955 Act was renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976. The Supreme Court held in the PUDR case (1982) that Article 17 operates against private individuals. Article 18 bars titles except military and academic ones; Balaji Raghavan (1995) held National Awards are not titles. Article 23 bans traffic in human beings and forced labour against the State and private persons. Article 24 bars employment of children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work. The Child Labour Act, 1986 was renamed in 2016.

Article 19 guarantees six freedoms to citizens, protected only against State action. The right to property in 19(1)(f) was deleted in 1978 and co-operative societies were added in 2011. Grounds of restriction on speech include sovereignty and integrity (16th Amendment, 1963) and public order (1st Amendment, 1951). Assembly must be peaceful, unarmed and on public land and does not include a right to strike. Association includes the negative right but not the right to recognition. In Anuradha Bhasin (2020) internet-based trade was protected under 19(1)(g), subject to proportionality.

Article 20 bars ex-post-facto criminal laws, double jeopardy and self-incrimination. The ex-post-facto bar does not cover civil or tax laws, and self-incrimination excludes blood specimens and signatures. Article 22 gives a person arrested under ordinary law the right to grounds, a lawyer and production before a magistrate within 24 hours. Preventive detention beyond three months needs an advisory board of high court judges; the 44th Amendment's two months is not in force. Parliament alone legislates on defence, foreign affairs and the security of India, while other grounds are concurrent. Laws such as PDA 1950, MISA, TADA and POTA were expired or repealed.

Article 21 is available to citizens and non-citizens. Gopalan (1950) read it narrowly against executive action only, and Maneka Gandhi (1978) overruled it, introducing in effect due process. The Court has listed many rights under Article 21, such as privacy, shelter, livelihood and passive euthanasia. Cases such as Olga Tellis (livelihood) and Puttaswamy (privacy) are linked with those rights. Article 21A, added by the 86th Amendment (2002), gives free and compulsory education to children aged six to fourteen. The RTE Act, 2009 came into force on 1 April 2010.

Article 25 protects individuals and Article 26 religious denominations, which must meet three conditions. The right to propagate does not include conversion. Article 27 bars taxes, not fees, for promoting a religion. Article 28 prohibits religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions and makes it voluntary in recognised and aided ones. Article 29 protects any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture. Article 30 protects minorities' educational institutions, and the term minority is undefined.

Article 32 is a basic feature, called by Ambedkar the heart and soul of the Constitution. It can be suspended only as the Constitution provides, as under Article 359. Its jurisdiction is original but not exclusive and is concurrent with Article 226. The Supreme Court issues writs only for Fundamental Rights, while a high court may also do so for other purposes. Habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo-warranto each have their own limits. Quo-warranto can be sought by any public-minded person.

Article 33 lets Parliament alone restrict the rights of the armed forces, police and similar forces. Article 34 deals with martial law, which is implicit in the Constitution and differs from a National Emergency. Article 35 vests power in Parliament alone to legislate for certain rights. The right to property was repealed in 1978 and survives as Article 300A. Article 31A saves five categories of laws from Articles 14 and 19, and Article 31B shields the Ninth Schedule. Coelho (2007) denied blanket immunity to the Ninth Schedule, and Minerva Mills (1980) struck down the extension of Article 31C.

concepts.description: Nature of Part IV, Articles 36 and 37, why the Directives are non-justiciable.
concepts.rule: Part IV runs from Article 36 to 51 and the idea came from the Irish Constitution of 1937. Article 36 gives 'State' the Part III meaning and Article 37 calls the principles fundamental in governance though not enforceable by courts. They resemble the 1935 instrument of instructions. The framers made them non-justiciable for lack of resources, diversity and the State's need for freedom of timing. Sir B.N. Rau proposed the justiciable/non-justiciable division. Fundamental Rights are negative and justiciable, whereas the Directives are positive and non-justiciable.
concepts.example: Courts cannot strike a law down for violating a Directive but may uphold it for giving effect to one.

concepts.rule: Critics: K.T. Shah, Nasiruddin, T.T. Krishnamachari, Wheare and Jennings on no legal force. Srinivasan and Jennings: illogically arranged. Jennings: conservative, Fabian Socialism without the socialism. Santhanam: constitutional conflict. Defenders: Singhvi, Chagla, Ambedkar, Austin, Rau and Setalvad. Roles include continuity of policy, filling the gap in Part III and a test of government performance.
concepts.example: Setalvad called the Directives beacon-lights to the courts in judicial review.

concepts.rule: The Constitution has no classification; the three groups are by content and direction. Socialistic: Arts 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47. Gandhian: Arts 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48. Liberal-intellectual: Arts 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51. Articles 43, 47 and 48 appear in two groups.
concepts.example: Article 44, the uniform civil code, is a liberal-intellectual principle.

concepts.name: Amendments to the Directive Principles and Directives outside Part IV
concepts.rule: The 42nd Amendment (1976) added four Directives: Arts 39 (children), 39A, 43A and 48A. The 44th (1978) added the minimising of inequalities in Art 38. The 86th (2002) changed Art 45 to early childhood care and created Art 21A. The 97th (2011) added Art 43B. Outside Part IV: Art 335, 350-A and 351, also non-justiciable.
concepts.example: Article 351 makes it a duty of the Union to promote Hindi.

concepts.rule: Champakam Dorairajan (1951): FRs prevail, but Parliament may amend them. Golak Nath (1967): FRs cannot be amended to implement Directives. The 24th and 25th Amendments (1971) responded to Golak Nath; Art 31C shielded laws implementing Art 39(b),(c) from challenge under Arts 14, 19 and 31. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) struck down the second provision of Art 31C but upheld the first. The 42nd Amendment extension was struck down in Minerva Mills (1980), which stressed the balance of the two.
concepts.example: Minerva Mills compared the two Parts to two wheels of a chariot.

concepts.rule: The Planning Commission (1950) was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015. Land reform, the Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 (since renamed), labour laws, nationalisation and the Legal Services Authorities Act (1987) are cited. Lok adalat awards are final with no appeal. The Criminal Procedure Code (1973), a historical account since the Code has been replaced by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, separated the judiciary from the executive. The 73rd Amendment gave panchayati raj constitutional status. Incomplete implementation is blamed on finances, conditions, population and Centre-state relations.
concepts.example: The Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 and Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 serve the environment Directive.

concepts.rule: Article 368 in Part XX deals with the powers of Parliament to amend the Constitution and its procedure, and Parliament acts in exercise of its constituent power by addition, variation or repeal; it cannot amend the basic structure, as ruled in Kesavananda Bharati (1973). The procedure is neither as easy as Britain's nor as difficult as the USA's, so the Constitution is a synthesis of flexible and rigid. An amendment bill can be introduced only in either House of Parliament, not in the state legislatures, by a minister or a private member and without the President's prior permission. It must be passed in each House separately by a special majority, a majority of the total membership and two-thirds of the members present and voting, with no provision for a joint sitting on disagreement. A bill amending federal provisions must also be ratified by the legislatures of half the states by a simple majority. The President must then give assent, neither withholding it nor returning the bill, as the 24th Amendment Act of 1971 made obligatory, and the Constitution stands amended according to the Act.
concepts.example: A bill to change the lists of the Seventh Schedule is passed by a special majority in each House, ratified by half of the state legislatures, and then receives the President's obligatory assent.

concepts.rule: India has no special body such as a Constitutional Convention or Constitutional Assembly for amendment; the constituent power is vested in Parliament and in few cases in the state legislatures, which, can initiate nothing except a resolution asking Parliament to create or abolish a legislative council. Apart from the special majority, amendment bills are passed like ordinary bills, but a joint sitting is available for an ordinary bill and not for an amendment bill. Some matters are changed by a simple majority outside Article 368 and are not deemed amendments for its purposes. In Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1964) the Supreme Court held that 'law' in Article 13 means only ordinary law and not constituent law, so Parliament could amend Fundamental Rights; Golak Nath (1967) reversed this, holding Fundamental Rights 'transcendental and immutable'. Parliament's 24th Amendment (1971) amended Articles 13 and 368 to restore its power, and Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled Golak Nath and upheld that Act.
concepts.example: A resolution of a state legislature asking Parliament to abolish its legislative council is the only proposal a state legislature can send, and Parliament may approve it, reject it or do nothing.

concepts.rule: Article 368 provides two types of amendment, special majority and special majority with ratification by half the states, while other articles allow amendment by a simple majority of Parliament, which is not deemed an amendment for Article 368; hence the Constitution can be amended in three ways. The simple-majority matters include new states and boundaries, legislative councils, the Second Schedule, quorum, MPs' salaries, citizenship, elections, delimitation, Union territories and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules. Most provisions, including Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, need a special majority, where 'total membership' means the House as constituted, irrespective of vacancies or absentees. Federal provisions, such as the election of the President, the executive power of the Union and the states, the Supreme Court and high courts, legislative distribution, the GST Council added by the 101st Amendment (2016), the Seventh Schedule lists, representation of states and Article 368 itself, also need consent of half the state legislatures by simple majority, with no time limit and no effect from the inaction of the rest.
concepts.example: Fixing the quorum in Parliament needs only a simple majority, a change to Fundamental Rights needs a special majority, and a change to the lists of the Seventh Schedule also needs the consent of half the states.

concepts.description: The seven grounds of criticism, the defence of the procedure, and the remarks of Nehru, Ambedkar and Wheare.
concepts.idea: Critics fault the procedure for vesting everything in Parliament, leaving gaps on the states and the Houses, but it is judged a good balance between flexibility and rigidity.
concepts.rule: Critics point out that there is no special amending body, that state legislatures cannot initiate amendments except the council resolution, that most of the Constitution can be amended by Parliament alone and that only half of the states (three-fourths in the USA) are needed in few cases. They add that no time frame is set for state ratification and the Constitution is silent on withdrawal of approval, that there is no joint sitting for a deadlock unlike for an ordinary bill, that the process resembles ordinary legislation, and that the sketchy provisions invite litigation. Despite these defects the procedure is regarded as simple, successful and neither so flexible as to allow whims nor so rigid as to be incapable of adapting, a balance Wheare endorsed. Nehru said there is no permanence in a Constitution; Ambedkar said the Assembly provided a facile procedure unlike Canada, America or Australia; Wheare called the variety wise but rare.
concepts.example: Nehru warned that a rigid and permanent Constitution would stop the growth of a living people, a view cited in favour of a flexible procedure.

concepts.rule: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled Golak Nath and upheld the 24th Amendment, allowing Parliament to abridge Fundamental Rights, but laid down that its constituent power under Article 368 cannot alter the basic structure. Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975) applied the doctrine to invalidate a 39th Amendment provision keeping election disputes of the Prime Minister and Speaker out of the courts. The 42nd Amendment (1976) declared no limit on the constituent power and barred any court challenge; Minerva Mills (1980) invalidated this as it excluded judicial review, a basic feature, and held that a limited amending power is itself a basic feature. Waman Rao (1980) applied the doctrine to amendments after April 24, 1973. Today Parliament may amend any part including Fundamental Rights without affecting the basic structure, which the Supreme Court is yet to define, though about twenty elements have emerged and the table of basic-structure elements maps them to cases.
concepts.example: A law that removes the courts' power to review a constitutional amendment would be struck down because judicial review is a basic feature, as in Minerva Mills.

concepts.rule: Parliament can legislate for the whole or any part of India and alone makes extra-territorial laws, while a state law applies outside the state only with a sufficient nexus. The President makes regulations for certain union territories, and the Governor or President can direct that an Act not apply to scheduled or tribal areas. The Union List has 98 subjects, the State List 59 and the Concurrent List 52, and the 42nd Amendment moved five subjects to the Concurrent List. Residuary powers lie with Parliament, as in Canada, unlike the 1935 Act which gave them to the Governor-General. Union List prevails over State and Concurrent Lists and the Concurrent over the State List; a state law with Presidential assent prevails in that state but Parliament may override it later. The 101st Amendment gave concurrent GST powers and Parliament exclusive power over inter-state supplies.
concepts.example: A state law on a Concurrent subject that received Presidential assent prevails in that state until Parliament subsequently legislates on the same matter.

concepts.rule: Parliament may legislate on State List matters (and GST) on a Rajya Sabha resolution backed by two-thirds of members present and voting, in force one year at a time and renewable. It may also do so during a national emergency, at the request of two or more states, to implement international agreements, and during President's rule. Laws under the Rajya Sabha resolution or emergency cease six months after they end, whereas a law made in President's rule continues and can be altered by the state legislature. A state request makes the law applicable to the requesting states and operates as abdication of state power. The Centre controls state legislation through reservation of bills for the President, Article 304 sanction, financial emergency directions and Governor's ordinance limits.
concepts.example: The Geneva Convention Act, 1960 implements an international obligation, whereas the Prize Competition Act, 1955 was passed on state requests.

concepts.rule: The Centre's executive power covers Union List subjects and treaty rights, a state's covers the State List, and on Concurrent subjects it rests with the states unless Constitution or Parliament confers it on the Centre. States must comply with Parliament's laws and not impede Central executive power; non-compliance with directions can lead to President's rule via Article 365. The Centre may direct states on communications of national importance, railway protection, mother-tongue instruction and Scheduled Tribe schemes. Delegation is by agreement with consent, or by a law of Parliament without consent, which a state legislature cannot do. Cooperation devices include water-dispute adjudication, the Inter-State Council (set up 1990) and full faith and credit. Emergencies and Article 355 increase Central control.
concepts.example: The Essential Commodities Act is made on a Concurrent subject yet vests executive power in the Centre.

concepts.rule: The IAS, IPS and IFoS are recruited and trained by the Centre, controlled jointly, and form a single service with uniform pay; new services need a Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 312. They restrict state autonomy but are defended for standards, uniformity and liaison. A state PSC's members are appointed by the Governor and removed only by the President; Parliament can set up a Joint State PSC and the UPSC can serve states on request. India has an integrated judiciary, and Parliament can establish a common high court. Non-constitutional advisory bodies such as NITI Aayog and conferences like the governors' and chief ministers' conferences promote coordination.
concepts.example: The chief ministers' conference is presided over by the Prime Minister and the chief secretaries' by the cabinet secretary.

concepts.rule: Parliament taxes Union List subjects, states taxes State List subjects, there are no tax entries in the Concurrent List except GST, and residuary taxes lie with Parliament. States face limits such as the Rs 2,500 profession tax ceiling. Article 268 duties are levied by the Centre and collected and appropriated by states; Article 269 taxes are assigned to states; Article 269A covers inter-state GST; Article 270 taxes are shared on Finance Commission advice; Article 271 surcharges go to the Centre alone. The 80th Amendment followed the 10th Finance Commission's 29 per cent scheme and the 101st Amendment introduced GST. The GST Council under Article 279-A recommends rates, exemptions and model laws.
concepts.example: Stamp duties on cheques and promissory notes are levied by the Centre but collected and appropriated by the state in which levied.

concepts.rule: Article 275 statutory grants go to needy states on the Finance Commission's advice, while Article 282 grants are discretionary. The Finance Commission under Article 280 is quasi-judicial, constituted every fifth year or earlier, and is the balancing wheel of fiscal federalism. Certain tax bills need the President's recommendation and the CAG certifies net proceeds. The Centre can borrow within or outside India, states only within India, and states need Central consent while Central loans are outstanding. Central property is exempt from state tax, state property from Central tax, but companies and local authorities are not exempt, and customs and excise duties are not covered by state immunity. In a national emergency the President can reduce or cancel transfers, and in a financial emergency the Centre can direct salary reductions.
concepts.example: The Centre can levy customs duty on goods imported by a state, according to the 1963 advisory opinion.

concepts.rule: Relations were smooth till 1967; after Congress lost nine states, non-Congress governments demanded autonomy and resources. Fourteen tension areas are listed, from governors to Central agencies. The First ARC (1966, Morarji Desai, then K. Hanumanthayya) reported in 1969 with 22 recommendations after a Setalvad study team, and no action followed. The Tamil Nadu Government's Rajamannar Committee (appointed 1969, reported 1971) recommended a permanent Finance Commission, omitting Articles 356, 357 and 365, and state residuary powers. The Akali Dal's 1973 Anandpur Sahib Resolution and the 1977 West Bengal Memorandum sought a narrow Centre; the Centre did not accept the West Bengal demands.
concepts.example: The West Bengal Memorandum of 1977 wanted 75 per cent of the Centre's revenue to be allocated to the states.

concepts.rule: The three-member Sarkaria Commission (1983, reported 1988) found the constitutional arrangements sound, rejected curtailing the Centre, and made 247 recommendations, of which 180 were implemented, most importantly the Inter-State Council in 1990. It recommended sparing use of Article 356, strengthened All-India Services and reactivated zonal councils. The Punchhi Commission (2007, reported 2010, 1,456 pages) concluded cooperative federalism was the key and made over 310 recommendations. They covered governors' tenure and selection, hung-assembly guidelines, localised emergency, new All-India Services and fiscal reforms.
concepts.example: Sarkaria wanted the NDC renamed the National Economic and Development Council, while Punchhi proposed a framework for localised emergency.

concepts.rule: The Emergency provisions are in Part XVIII (Articles 352 to 360) and make the federal system work as a unitary one without a formal amendment. The Constitution stipulates three emergencies: Article 352 (war, external aggression or armed rebellion; the Constitution calls it 'proclamation of emergency'), Article 356 (failure of constitutional machinery in states) and Article 360 (financial). The President can proclaim a National Emergency even before the event if satisfied that there is imminent danger; the 38th Amendment (1975) allowed different proclamations on different grounds, the 42nd (1976) allowed limiting it to a part of India, and the 44th (1978) replaced 'internal disturbance' by 'armed rebellion' and required the written recommendation of the Cabinet. The 38th Amendment's immunity from judicial review was deleted by the 44th, and Minerva Mills (1980) held that a proclamation can be challenged for malafide, wholly extraneous or irrelevant facts, or absurdity or perversity.

The proclamation must be approved by both Houses within one month (originally two months; reduced by the 44th Amendment). If the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the proclamation survives until 30 days from the first sitting of the reconstituted Lok Sabha, provided the Rajya Sabha has meanwhile approved it. Once approved it continues for six months and can be extended indefinitely with approval every six months (added by the 44th Amendment; earlier it could last as long as the Cabinet desired). Every approving resolution needs a special majority (majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting). The President may revoke it any time by a subsequent proclamation without approval, and must revoke it if the Lok Sabha passes a resolution of disapproval, for which a special sitting must be held within 14 days on the written notice of one-tenth of its members.

Effects are grouped as Centre-state relations (executive, legislative, financial), the life of the Lok Sabha and state assemblies, and Fundamental Rights. The Centre can direct any state on any matter, but state governments are not suspended. Parliament can legislate on the State List, the state legislature is not suspended but is subject to Parliament's overriding power, such laws become inoperative six months after the Emergency ceases, and the President can issue ordinances on state subjects when Parliament is not in session. The 42nd Amendment extended the executive and legislative consequences to any other state. The President can reduce or cancel financial transfers to the states till the end of the financial year in which the Emergency ceases, and the order is laid before both Houses. The life of the Lok Sabha or an assembly can be extended by law one year at a time, not beyond six months after the Emergency ceases.

Articles 358 and 359 describe the effect of a National Emergency on the Fundamental Rights. Under Article 358 the six rights of Article 19 are automatically suspended on proclamation, no separate order is needed, the State may make any law or take any executive action abridging them, and Article 19 revives when the Emergency ceases, though no remedy lies for what was done. Article 359 authorises the President to suspend the right to move any court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights; the rights are not suspended, only their enforcement, only for those named in the Presidential Order, for the Emergency or a shorter period, for the whole or part of the country. The 44th Amendment confined Article 358 to an Emergency on war or external aggression, barred suspension of the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21, and limited the protection to laws related to the Emergency and executive action taken under them. Article 359 operates in both External and Internal Emergencies.

Article 355 imposes a duty on the Centre to protect every state and ensure its government is carried on according to the Constitution; Article 356 is invoked on the Governor's report or otherwise, and Article 365 permits the President to hold that machinery has failed if a state does not comply with a Centre's direction. The proclamation must be approved by both Houses within two months by a simple majority, continues for six months and can be extended with approval every six months up to three years. Beyond one year, extension needs a National Emergency in operation and an Election Commission certificate that elections cannot be held (44th Amendment). The President takes over the state government's functions, may declare that Parliament will exercise the legislature's powers, the council of ministers is dismissed, the assembly is suspended or dissolved, Parliament may delegate law-making to the President, and the High Court is untouched. Laws so made continue after the Rule unless repealed, altered or re-enacted by the state legislature.

President's Rule has been imposed on more than 125 occasions since 1950, first in Punjab in 1951, often arbitrarily. The Janata Government in 1977 and the Congress in 1980 each imposed it in nine states on the ground that the assemblies no longer represented the electorate. In 1992 it was imposed in three BJP-ruled states, which Bommai (1994) upheld because secularism is a basic feature; the Nagaland (1988), Karnataka (1989) and Meghalaya (1991) impositions were not upheld. The 38th Amendment made the President's satisfaction final and the 44th deleted that. Bommai held that the proclamation is justiciable, the Centre must prove relevant material, the court cannot examine its adequacy, it can restore the dismissed government, the assembly can only be suspended until Parliament approves, loss of majority is tested on the floor, and a new party at the Centre cannot dismiss other ministries. Proper and improper uses were listed from the Sarkaria Commission.

Article 360 empowers the President to proclaim a Financial Emergency if the financial stability or credit of India or any part of its territory is threatened. The 38th Amendment made the President's satisfaction final and conclusive, but the 44th Amendment deleted that, so it is open to judicial review. The proclamation must be approved by both Houses within two months (with the usual 30-day rule if the Lok Sabha is dissolved), by a simple majority; once approved it continues until revoked, with no maximum period and no repeated approval, and the President may revoke it by a subsequent proclamation. The Centre may direct states to observe financial propriety, including reduction of salaries and reservation of money and financial bills for the President; the President may direct reduction of salaries of persons serving the Union, including judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts. Ambedkar likened it to a US measure of 1933; none has been declared so far, though there was a financial crisis in 1991.

concepts.description: The 1962, 1971 and 1975 National Emergencies, the Shah Commission and the 44th Amendment, the Constituent Assembly debate for and against the Emergency provisions, and the Articles that deal with Emergencies.
concepts.rule: A National Emergency has been proclaimed three times. The first, in October 1962, followed Chinese aggression in the NEFA and was in force till January 1968, so no fresh proclamation was needed in 1965. The second, in December 1971, followed the attack by Pakistan; a third, in June 1975, was made while it was in operation, and both were revoked in March 1977. The first two were on external aggression; the third on internal disturbance, and proved the most controversial. After the Janata Party came to power in 1977 the Shah Commission was appointed, did not justify the declaration, and the 44th Amendment (1978) added safeguards. In the Constituent Assembly, critics (Kamath, K.T. Shah, T.T. Krishnamachari, Kunzru) feared a dictatorship and loss of federal and financial autonomy, while Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar and Mahabir Tyagi defended the provisions and Ambedkar accepted that they might be abused.

concepts.description: The electoral college, the weighting of votes, the single transferable vote and disputes about the election.
concepts.rule: The college consists of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament, of the state legislative assemblies and of the assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry (added by the 70th Amendment); nominated members and members of legislative councils do not vote, and members of a dissolved assembly cease to be qualified. An MLA's vote value is the population of the state (1971 census, per the 84th Amendment) divided by the total number of elected members of its assembly, then counted in multiples of one thousand; an MP's vote value is the total value of MLA votes divided by the elected members of both Houses (700 in the 2022 election, from the state-wise electoral college table). Voting is by secret ballot, with preferences marked 1, 2, 3; the quota is the valid votes divided by (seats plus one), plus one, and the lowest candidate's votes are transferred until the quota is reached. The Supreme Court decides all disputes; the election cannot be challenged because the college was incomplete, and acts done before a void declaration stay valid. Indirect election was chosen because the President is a nominal executive and direct election would be costly.

concepts.description: Eligibility, nomination rules, the oath, conditions of office, emoluments and immunities.
Term, re-election, impeachment procedure, vacancies and who acts as President.
The executive, legislative, financial, judicial, diplomatic, military and emergency powers.
The three vetoes over Central and state bills.
Article 123, its four limitations, judicial review and the Wadhwa case.
Article 72, the five forms of clemency, the Governor's power and the Kehar Singh and Maru Ram principles.
The President as nominal executive, Articles 53, 74 and 75, the 42nd and 44th Amendments and situational discretion.

concepts.rule: Article 75 says only that the President appoints the Prime Minister; by convention the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha is appointed. When no party has a clear majority, or the Prime Minister dies suddenly with no obvious successor, the President may use personal discretion (Charan Singh, 1979; Rajiv Gandhi, 1984), but must appoint the leader whom the ruling party elects. The Delhi High Court (1980) held that a majority need not be proved before appointment, and the Supreme Court (1996) allowed a non-member to be Prime Minister for six months. The Prime Minister may belong to either House, whereas in Britain the Prime Minister must be in the House of Commons.

The President administers the oaths of office and secrecy before the Prime Minister enters office; the oath of office has four undertakings and the form is similar to that of any Union minister. The term is not fixed and the Prime Minister holds office during the pleasure of the President, but cannot be dismissed while enjoying majority support in the Lok Sabha. On losing its confidence the Prime Minister must resign or can be dismissed (V.P. Singh 1990, Deve Gowda 1997). Salary and allowances are determined by Parliament; the Prime Minister gets those of an MP plus a sumptuary allowance, free accommodation, travelling allowance and medical facilities.

The Prime Minister recommends the persons the President may appoint as ministers, allocates and reshuffles portfolios, and can ask a minister to resign or advise the President to dismiss him or her. He or she presides over the council, guides and coordinates all ministers, and can bring about its collapse by resigning. The resignation or death of the Prime Minister dissolves the council (in practice the outgoing council is usually asked to continue until a successor is sworn in); that of any other minister merely creates a vacancy. The Prime Minister chairs NITI Aayog (which succeeded the Planning Commission), the National Integration Council, the Inter-State Council and the National Water Resources Council, shapes foreign policy, is chief spokesman, political-level crisis manager, party leader and political head of the services.

The Prime Minister is the principal channel of communication between the President and the council of ministers (Article 78) and advises the President, on the appointment of the Attorney General, the CAG, the chairman and members of the UPSC, election commissioners and the chairman and members of the Finance Commission (since the 2023 Act, election commissioners are appointed on the recommendation of a selection committee that includes the Prime Minister). As leader of the Lower House the Prime Minister advises on summoning and proroguing sessions, can recommend dissolution of the Lok Sabha at any time, and announces government policies on the floor of the House. Article 75 provides that the Prime Minister is appointed by the President, ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President and the council is collectively responsible to the House of the People.

concepts.idea: Writers on Britain describe the Prime Minister as a dominant figure, and the same holds good in India.
concepts.rule: Lord Morley called the Prime Minister 'primus inter pares' and 'key stone of the cabinet arch', holding a position of exceptional and peculiar authority. Harcourt called him 'a moon among lesser stars'; Jennings 'a sun around which planets revolve' with all roads leading to him; Laski the pivot of the governmental machinery, central to the cabinet's formation, life and death; Greaves the master of the Government; Munro the captain of the ship of the state. Crossman spoke of Prime Ministerial government and Berkely of the Prime Minister's super-ministerial powers; this holds good in India, and Ambedkar compared the Prime Minister, not the President, with the US President.

Six people (Morarji Desai, Charan Singh, V.P. Singh, P.V. Narasimha Rao, H.D. Deve Gowda and Narendra Modi) became Prime Ministers after being Chief Ministers; Desai was the first non-Congress Prime Minister (March 1977) and Rao the first from South India. The Constitution contains no provision for a caretaker government; the term describes a council that has lost confidence or been dissolved but is asked to continue. It manages routine business and makes no significant policy decisions except on national security or interest. The Tarkunde Committee (1974-75), the communique of President Reddy (August 1979) and the Calcutta High Court (December 1979) support these limits.

Article 74 provides a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President, who shall act in accordance with such advice. The President may require reconsideration but must act on the advice tendered after it; the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976 made the advice binding and the 44th Act of 1978 added the proviso. The advice tendered by ministers cannot be inquired into in any court. Article 77: executive action is expressed in the name of the President, authenticated orders cannot be questioned on that ground, and the President makes the rules for business and its allocation. Article 78 makes it the Prime Minister's duty to communicate Council decisions, furnish information and submit matters on the President's requirement. Article 88 lets a minister speak and take part in either House, a joint sitting and committees but not vote. In U.N.R. Rao (1971) the council did not cease on dissolution of the Lok Sabha and Article 74 was mandatory; in Shamsher Singh (1974) the President's satisfaction was held to be the council's.

The Prime Minister is appointed by the President and other ministers on the Prime Minister's advice. The total number of ministers including the Prime Minister cannot exceed 15% of the Lok Sabha, and a defector disqualified from Parliament is barred from ministership, both by the 91st Amendment Act of 2003. A non-member can be a minister but must become a member of either House within six months, by election or nomination. The President administers the oaths of office and secrecy, and the office oath has four limbs. In 1990 the Supreme Court upheld Devi Lal's oath as Deputy Prime Minister, the description being descriptive only. Parliament determines salaries; the 1952 Act applies and in 2001 the sumptuary allowance was raised to Rs 3,000, 2,000, 1,000 and 600 by rank.

Article 75 makes the Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; all ministers, including those from the Rajya Sabha, resign when a no-confidence motion is passed, and the Prime Minister's resignation is the council's. The council may advise dissolution of the Lok Sabha, but the President may not oblige a council that has lost confidence. Cabinet decisions bind all ministers, and a dissenting minister who will not defend them must resign, as Ambedkar, Deshmukh and Arif Mohammed did. Ministers hold office during the President's pleasure, and the President removes a minister only on the Prime Minister's advice, even if the council enjoys confidence. India has no legal responsibility of ministers, no countersignature is needed, and courts cannot inquire into the advice, unlike Britain.

The council consists of cabinet ministers, ministers of state and deputy ministers, differing in rank, emoluments and political importance, with the Prime Minister at the top; a deputy prime minister is appointed mostly for political reasons. Ministers of state may have independent charge or be attached to cabinet ministers; they are not cabinet members. Deputy ministers have no independent charge. Parliamentary secretaries are not council members and are appointed by the Prime Minister. the council is wider, does not meet as a body and implements decisions, while the cabinet is smaller, meets weekly and directs; the cabinet entered Article 352 through the 44th Amendment Act in 1978.

The cabinet is the highest decision-making authority, chief policy body, supreme executive authority, chief coordinator and crisis manager, controls higher appointments and deals with foreign affairs; its advice binds the President. Writers describe it as the steering wheel (Muir), keystone (Lowell), pivot (Marriott), solar orb (Gladstone), magnet of policy (Barker) and hyphen and buckle (Bagehot); Muir called its position a dictatorship only qualified by publicity. The Kitchen Cabinet is an informal, extra-constitutional inner circle of the Prime Minister that may include outsiders and was powerful under Indira Gandhi. Its merits are efficiency, speed and secrecy; its demerits lowered cabinet authority and bypassing the legal process; it also exists in the USA and Britain.

concepts.description: The strength, composition and sources of members of the Rajya Sabha and the Lok Sabha.
concepts.rule: Parliament consists of the President, the Council of States and the House of the People; the President is an integral part though not a member. The Rajya Sabha has a maximum of 250 (238 elected indirectly, 12 nominated) and at present 245: 225 states, 8 union territories, 12 nominated; seats follow population, by single transferable vote. Only Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu & Kashmir have Rajya Sabha seats. The Lok Sabha has a maximum of 550 (530 states, 20 union territories) and at present 543 (524 and 19), directly elected; voting age was lowered to 18 by the 61st Amendment. Anglo-Indian nomination ceased on 25 January 2020 after the 104th Amendment. Seats and SC/ST reservations are fixed state-wise.

Seats are allotted so the seats-to-population ratio is the same for all states (except states under six million), and each state is divided so that constituencies are uniform. Readjustment follows each census under Delimitation Commission Acts of 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002; the 42nd Amendment froze seats at the 1971 level till 2000 and the 84th Amendment extended it by 25 years (the freeze is stated as up to 2026 and runs to the first census taken after 2026), while the 87th Amendment based delimitation on the 2001 census. SC/ST seats are reserved by population ratio, until 2030 under the 104th Amendment, with no separate electorate. The Lok Sabha uses first-past-the-post in single-member constituencies; proportional representation (single transferable vote or list system) was not adopted for reasons of literacy and party multiplication.

concepts.description: Tenure of the two Houses, sessions, adjournment, prorogation, dissolution and lapse of bills.
concepts.rule: The Rajya Sabha is a continuing chamber; one-third retire every second year and members serve six years under the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The Lok Sabha's term is five years from its first meeting; it can be extended during a national emergency, one year at a time, but not beyond six months after the emergency. The President summons the Houses, with no more than six months between sessions. Adjournment ends a sitting and is done by the presiding officer; prorogation ends a session and is done by the President. On dissolution a bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses, while a bill pending in the Rajya Sabha and not passed by the Lok Sabha does not lapse.

A member must be a citizen, at least 30 (Rajya Sabha) or 25 (Lok Sabha) years old, and take an oath before a person authorised by the Election Commission. Disqualifications include an office of profit, unsound mind, insolvency and foreign citizenship; the Representation of the People Act adds conviction with two or more years' imprisonment, but not preventive detention. The President decides, on the Election Commission's opinion, while defection under the Tenth Schedule is decided by the Speaker or Chairman. A person elected to both Houses must opt within 10 days, or the Rajya Sabha seat falls vacant; absence for sixty days can vacate a seat. Sitting without the oath attracts a penalty of Rs 500 a day.

concepts.description: The Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Speaker Pro Tem and panel of chairpersons of the Lok Sabha.
concepts.rule: The Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha, resigns by writing to the Deputy Speaker and is removed by an effective majority after 14 days' notice. While a removal resolution is pending the Speaker cannot preside but may speak and vote in the first instance, not in a tie. The Speaker decides money bills, presides over joint sittings and decides defection cases subject to judicial review. The Deputy Speaker is not subordinate to the Speaker and becomes chairman of any committee he joins. The Speaker Pro Tem is appointed by the President and administers oath to members. Mavalankar was the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman, who is not a member and can be removed only by removal from the Vice-Presidency; he has no power to decide money bills or preside over a joint sitting. The Deputy Chairman is elected by the House, is not subordinate to the Chairman and is removed by an effective majority after 14 days' notice. The Leader of the House is in the Rules and the Leader of the Opposition in a 1977 statute, while the whip is only a convention. Under the 1998 Act a recognised party needs 55 Lok Sabha or 25 Rajya Sabha members. The Minister of Parliamentary Affairs is the government Chief Whip in the Lok Sabha.

The quorum is one-tenth of the House, i.e. 55 in the Lok Sabha and 25 in the Rajya Sabha. Questions are decided by a majority of members present and voting, the presiding officer using only a casting vote. Hindi and English are the languages of Parliament, English continuing under the Official Languages Act, 1963. Ministers and the Attorney General may speak but not vote in either House. A simple majority is the general rule (Article 100); effective majority means excluding vacancies; absolute majority is of the full strength; special majorities apply to amendment, impeachment and removals. A lame-duck session is the last session of the old Lok Sabha after a new one is elected.

Starred questions get oral answers with supplementaries, unstarred get written answers and short notice questions need under ten days' notice. The zero hour is an informal device unmentioned in the Rules, existing since 1962. The adjournment motion needs the support of 50 members, is not available in the Rajya Sabha and requires at least 2 hours 30 minutes of discussion. A no-confidence motion needs the support of 50 members; a censure motion can name individual ministers and need not lead to resignation. Closure may be simple, by compartments, kangaroo or guillotine. Half-an-hour and short duration discussions have no formal motion or vote.

A public bill is introduced by a minister on seven days' notice, a private bill by another member on one month's notice. An ordinary bill passes first, second and third readings in each House. The President may assent, withhold assent or return the bill once, and must assent if it is passed again, so has only a suspensive veto. A deadlock arises on rejection, final disagreement or six months of inaction, and the President may summon a joint sitting, not for money or Constitution amendment bills. The Speaker presides, and the joint sitting has been used thrice: the Dowry Prohibition Bill 1960, the Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill 1977 and the Prevention of Terrorism Bill 2002.

A bill is a money bill only if it contains solely the Article 110 matters, and fines, licence fees and local taxes alone do not make it one. The Speaker's decision is final, and the bill is introduced only in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation. The Rajya Sabha cannot amend or reject it and must return it within 14 days; the Lok Sabha may accept or reject its recommendations. The President may assent or withhold assent but cannot return it. A financial bill (I) is Lok Sabha-only but otherwise ordinary, and a financial bill (II) can start in either House and needs the President's recommendation at consideration.

The 'budget' is the annual financial statement of Article 112. No demand for a grant is made without the President's recommendation, and no money leaves the Consolidated Fund except under an appropriation law. The Rajya Sabha can only discuss the budget; voting on demands is the Lok Sabha's exclusive right, and charged expenditure is not voted. Cut motions are policy (Re 1), economy and token (Rs 100). A vote on account is generally for two months and one-sixth of the estimates. The Finance Bill must be enacted within 75 days. The Consolidated Fund needs appropriation, while the Public Account and Contingency Fund are operated by executive action.

Parliament legislates on the Union and residuary subjects and can legislate on the State List in five abnormal situations, including a Rajya Sabha resolution. Its constituent power is subject to the basic structure. The Rajya Sabha has special powers under Articles 249 and 312, can alone initiate removal of the Vice-President and can approve an emergency proclamation when the Lok Sabha is dissolved. Members cannot be arrested in civil cases during the session and 40 days before and after it. Breach of privilege is always contempt, but not conversely. Unlike the British Parliament, the Indian Parliament is limited by the written Constitution, federalism, judicial review and fundamental rights.

The Constitution mentions committees but leaves their composition, tenure and functions to the rules of the two Houses. A parliamentary committee is appointed or elected by the House or nominated by the Speaker/Chairman, works under his direction, reports to the House or to him and has a secretariat from the Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha; consultative committees fail these conditions. Standing committees are permanent and fall into six categories, while ad hoc committees are temporary and are inquiry or advisory committees. Select and joint committees on Bills are the advisory committees; the motion is moved and adopted in the House where the Bill is under consideration, and the Committee takes evidence, goes clause by clause and may carry notes of dissent. Consultative committees are chaired by the minister in charge, constituted by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs, have 10 to 30 members and stand dissolved with each Lok Sabha.

The committee was first set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act of 1919 and now has 22 members, 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha, elected every year by the single transferable vote; a minister cannot be a member. The Speaker appoints its chairman, and since 1967 by convention he is from the Opposition. It examines the CAG's audit reports, the appropriation and finance accounts, the accounts of state corporations and autonomous bodies audited by the CAG, and excess expenditure over grants, checking economy, prudence and propriety. The CAG is its guide, friend and philosopher. It conducts a post-mortem, does not decide policy, cannot disallow expenditure or issue orders, and its recommendations are advisory.

The first post-independence Estimates Committee was constituted in 1950 on John Mathai's recommendation; its 25 members became 30 in 1956, all from the Lok Sabha, elected every year, with the chairman generally from the ruling party. It suggests economies, alternative policies and the form of the estimates, and is called a continuous economy committee, but it lacks the CAG's assistance and its recommendations are advisory. The Committee on Public Undertakings was created in 1964 on the Krishna Menon Committee's recommendation with 15 members, raised to 22 (15 Lok Sabha, 7 Rajya Sabha) in 1974. It examines the reports and accounts of public undertakings and whether they follow sound business principles, but not major policy, day-to-day administration or matters under a special statute, and not more than ten to twelve undertakings a year.

concepts.description: Origin, objective, composition, jurisdiction, functions, procedure, merits and effectiveness of the DRSCs.
concepts.rule: Seventeen DRSCs were set up in 1993 on the Rules Committee of the Lok Sabha's recommendation and seven more in 2004 raised the number to 24; eight work under the Rajya Sabha and sixteen under the Lok Sabha. Their objective is greater accountability of the Executive, especially financial. Each has 31 members (21 Lok Sabha, 10 Rajya Sabha), nominated by the Speaker and the Chairman; a minister is not eligible and the term is one year. They consider demands for grants (without suggesting cut motions), bills, annual reports and long-term policy documents, but not day-to-day administration, and their recommendations are advisory. The ministries have by and large accepted their recommendations.

The Committee on Petitions examines petitions on bills and matters of public importance, the Committee of Privileges is semi-judicial, and the Ethics Committee, constituted in 1997 in the Rajya Sabha and in 2000 in the Lok Sabha, enforces the code of conduct. The Committee on Government Assurances (1953) follows up ministers' promises, the Committee on Subordinate Legislation (1953) checks delegated rule-making, and the Committee on Papers Laid on the Table (1975) checks papers against the Constitution, Act or Rule but leaves statutory notifications to the Subordinate Legislation committee. The SC/ST welfare committee and the Committee on Empowerment of Women (1997) have 30 members each, 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha. The Joint Committee on Offices of Profit has 15 members and recommends disqualification.

The Business Advisory Committee regulates the programme and time table (15 members in the Lok Sabha with the Speaker, 11 in the Rajya Sabha with the Chairman). The Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions is a Lok Sabha committee chaired by the Deputy Speaker; the Rajya Sabha's Business Advisory Committee does that work. The Rules Committee has 15 members in the Lok Sabha and 16 in the Rajya Sabha. The Committee on Absence of Members, for absence of 60 days or more, is in the Lok Sabha only. The General Purposes Committee is chaired by the presiding officer, the House Committee handles accommodation and amenities, the Library Committee has 9 members, and the Joint Committee on Salaries and Allowances, set up under the 1954 Act, has 15 members.

Article 143 lets the President seek the Court's opinion on (a) a question of law or fact of public importance (the Court may refuse) and (b) a dispute from a pre-constitution treaty or sanad (the Court must reply). The opinion is advisory, not binding. Fifteen references are listed from the Delhi Laws Act (1951) to the 2G spectrum case (2012). As a court of record, its judgements are preserved as precedents and it punishes contempt (in 1991 extended to high courts, subordinate courts and tribunals). The Contempt of Courts Act 1971 followed the H.N. Sanyal Committee; civil and criminal contempt; punishment up to six months or Rs 2,000 or both; one-year limitation; fair reporting and criticism exempt; not for Nyaya Panchayats.

Judicial review lets the Court declare ultra vires laws and executive orders of the Centre and states null and void. It can review its own judgements within thirty days before the same bench on new evidence, error on the face of the record or other sufficient reason; a curative petition on limited grounds (natural justice, miscarriage of justice, abuse of process, bias) survives a dismissed review. It is the ultimate interpreter of the Constitution, guided by doctrines such as severability and eclipse. Its other powers include enquiring into Public Service Commission members on a presidential reference (binding advice), withdrawing and transferring cases, binding all courts with its law and superintending all courts and tribunals. In comparison with the American Court, its judicial review is narrower than the American Court's and it follows 'procedure established by law' rather than 'due process of law'.

High courts began in 1862 at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras, with Allahabad added in 1866; the Seventh Amendment of 1956 let Parliament set up a common high court for two or more states, or states and a union territory. As per the standard count there were 25 high courts, only three of which have jurisdiction over more than one state; Delhi alone among the union territories has its own (since 1966), while Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh share one. Articles 214 to 231 deal with them. A high court consists of a chief justice and as many judges as the President thinks necessary, so its strength is not fixed by the Constitution. The chief justice is appointed by the President after consulting the Chief Justice of India and the governor; for other judges the chief justice of the high court is also consulted. The Second (1993) and Third (1998) Judges cases shaped the collegium, the 99th Amendment and NJAC Act of 2014 were struck down in 2015, and the collegium returned.

A high court judge must be a citizen of India who has held judicial office in India for ten years or has been a high court advocate for ten years; no minimum age is prescribed and, unlike for the Supreme Court, a distinguished jurist cannot be appointed. The oath is taken before the governor or a person he appoints. Parliament fixes salaries, allowances, privileges, leave and pension, which cannot be varied to the judge's disadvantage except during a financial emergency. A judge holds office until 62 (raised from 60 by the 15th Amendment of 1963), may resign in writing to the President, and vacates office on appointment to the Supreme Court or transfer to another high court. Removal is by the President on an address of each House by special majority, in the same session, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity; the Judges Enquiry Act (1968) requires a motion signed by 100 Lok Sabha or 50 Rajya Sabha members and a three-member committee.

The President may transfer a high court judge to another high court after consulting the Chief Justice of India; the judge receives a compensatory allowance fixed by Parliament. In 1977 the Supreme Court said transfers may be only an exceptional measure in public interest and not a punishment, and later that judicial review is necessary against arbitrary transfers, which, only the transferred judge can challenge. In the Third Judges case (1998) the Chief Justice of India was to consult the collegium of four senior-most Supreme Court judges and the chief justices of the two high courts concerned. The President may appoint an acting chief justice when the office is vacant or the chief justice is absent or unable to act, additional judges for up to two years to meet increased business or arrears, and acting judges for absent judges; additional and acting judges cannot serve beyond 62. A chief justice may, with the previous consent of the President and of the person, request a retired judge to sit temporarily; he enjoys the powers and privileges of a judge but is not otherwise deemed one.

concepts.description: The nine safeguards that protect high courts from executive and legislative pressure.
concepts.rule: Nine safeguards protect the independence of high courts. Judges are appointed by the President (in effect the cabinet) in consultation with the judiciary, which curtails executive discretion. They enjoy security of tenure: they can be removed only as the Constitution provides and do not hold office during the pleasure of the President. Salaries, allowances, privileges, leave and pension are fixed by Parliament and cannot be varied to their disadvantage except in a financial emergency. Judges' salaries and allowances, the staff's salaries, allowances and pensions and the court's administrative expenses are charged on the state's Consolidated Fund and are non-votable but can be discussed, while a judge's pension is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. Their conduct cannot be discussed in Parliament or a state legislature except during an impeachment motion; retired permanent judges cannot plead before any court or authority except the Supreme Court and other high courts; the court can punish for contempt; the chief justice appoints the staff; and jurisdiction specified in the Constitution cannot be curtailed by Parliament or the state legislature.

The Constitution keeps a high court's jurisdiction and powers the same as immediately before its commencement, adding revenue matters, writs and superintendence. Original jurisdiction covers election disputes of legislators, revenue matters, fundamental rights and cases transferred from subordinate courts involving interpretation of the Constitution; Calcutta, Bombay, Madras and Delhi also have original civil jurisdiction in cases of higher value, while the original criminal jurisdiction of the first three was abolished by the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973. Article 226 lets a high court issue writs for fundamental rights and for any other purpose, even outside its territory if the cause of action arises within it (15th Amendment, 1963); this is concurrent with Article 32 but wider, and the Chandra Kumar case (1997) made it part of the basic structure. Appellate jurisdiction is wider than original: first appeals on law and fact, second appeals on law only, intra-court appeals to a division bench, appeals from tribunals, and in criminal matters appeals where the sentence exceeds seven years, with confirmation of death sentences.

A high court has the power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals in its territory except military courts or tribunals: it can call for returns, make general rules, prescribe forms and settle fees. The power is broad, extending to courts whether or not subject to its appeals, covering administrative and judicial superintendence, revisional and suo motu, but it is extraordinary and used sparingly. The governor consults the high court on appointment, posting and promotion of district judges; the court handles posting, promotion, leave, transfer and discipline of other judicial service members, can withdraw a case involving a substantial constitutional question, and its law binds subordinate courts. As a court of record it keeps its proceedings as precedent and punishes contempt of itself and, under the Contempt of Courts Act 1971, of subordinate courts; it can review its own judgements. Judicial review under Articles 13 and 226 rests on three grounds; the 42nd Amendment curtailed it and the 43rd Amendment restored it.

Article 39A provides for free legal aid to the poor and weaker sections, and Articles 14 and 22(1) oblige the State to ensure equality before law and equal opportunity. The Legal Services Authorities Act, enacted in 1987, came into force on 9 November 1995. NALSA monitors and evaluates legal aid programmes and lays down policies, principles and schemes; State Legal Services Authorities, High Court Legal Services Committees, District Authorities, Taluk Committees and the Supreme Court Legal Services Committee carry them out. Their main functions are free legal services, Lok Adalats and rural legal awareness camps. Free services include court fees, lawyers, certified copies and preparation of appeals. Eligible persons include women and children, SC/ST members, industrial workmen, disaster victims, the disabled, persons in custody and, by income, those earning up to Rs 1 lakh (Rs 5 lakh in the Supreme Court Committee).

Lok Adalat means People's Court, based on Gandhian principles and part of ADR; the first post-independence camp was in Gujarat in 1982 and the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 gave it statutory status. The State, District, Supreme Court, High Court and Taluk legal services bodies may organise it; it generally has a judicial officer as chairman with a lawyer and a social worker. It settles cases pending before any court or matters not yet brought to court, but not offences that are not compoundable. A case may be referred if the parties agree, one party applies or the court is satisfied; pre-litigation disputes are referred by the organising agency on one party's application. It has civil court powers for summoning, discovery, affidavits and requisitioning records, and frames its own procedure. Its proceedings are deemed judicial proceedings (the reference is to the IPC 1860, now the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023). Its award is deemed a civil court decree, final and binding, with no appeal.

There are three types of Lok Adalats: National (held on one day in all courts from the Supreme Court to the Taluk level, monthly on a subject since 2015,), State or Regular (Continuous, Daily, Mobile and Mega) and Permanent. Their benefits include no court fee (refunded if paid), procedural flexibility, direct interaction with the judge, and a binding, non-appealable award. The Legal Services Authorities Act was amended in 2002 to create Permanent Lok Adalats for public utility services such as transport, postal and telephone services, power, water, sanitation, hospitals and insurance. Its chairman is or has been a district judge or higher, with two persons experienced in public utility services. Its pecuniary limit was Rs ten lakh and became Rs one crore in 2015; it has no jurisdiction over non-compoundable offences, bars courts after an application, and its award is final and by majority.

The Family Courts Act, 1984 provides for Family Courts to promote conciliation and speedy settlement of disputes relating to marriage and family affairs. They were demanded by women's associations and backed by the Law Commission's 59th Report (1974); the Code of Civil Procedure was amended in 1976 but courts made little use of it. State Governments establish them in consultation with the High Courts and must do so in every city or town with a population exceeding one million. They exclusively hear matrimonial relief, property of the spouses, legitimacy, guardianship and custody, and maintenance of wife, children and parents. The Court must first try reconciliation, with informal proceedings and counsellors, the parties have no right to a lawyer, evidence rules are simplified, and only one appeal lies, to the High Court.

The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 provides access to justice at the doorstep, drawing on Article 39A and the Law Commission's 114th Report. A Gram Nyayalaya is a court of Judicial Magistrate of the first class, presided over by a Nyayadhikari appointed by the State Government in consultation with the High Court, with the same salary and powers as First Class Magistrates. It is set up for every intermediate-level Panchayat or group of contiguous Panchayats, is a mobile court with civil and criminal powers over matters in the First and Second Schedules, follows summary procedure in criminal trial, uses conciliators and is not bound, by the Indian Evidence Act (since replaced by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023). Criminal appeals go to the Court of Session and civil appeals to the District Court, each within six months; plea bargaining is allowed. States establish them in consultation with High Courts; the Act does not make it mandatory, and the 2013 Conference left the decision to them.

The Commercial Courts Act, 2015 provides for Commercial Courts, Commercial Appellate Courts, and a Commercial Division and Commercial Appellate Division in High Courts to decide commercial disputes of specified value, defined as disputes from ordinary transactions of merchants, bankers, financiers and traders. It rests on the Law Commission's 253rd Report and aims at early resolution of high value disputes and investor confidence. The State Government constitutes Commercial Courts at district level and designates Commercial Appellate Courts at district judge level, while the Chief Justice constitutes the Commercial Division and Commercial Appellate Division in High Courts with ordinary original civil jurisdiction. The specified value is not less than Rs 3 lakh, reduced in 2018 from Rs 1 crore.
