Mediation is compulsory before a suit that does not contemplate urgent interim relief, and Legal Services Authorities may be empowered for it.

The Balwantrai Mehta Committee (reported November 1957) recommended a three-tier system; Rajasthan began it on 2 October 1959 at Nagaur, followed by Andhra Pradesh. The Ashok Mehta Committee (1978) proposed a two-tier system with a mandal panchayat. The G.V.K. Rao Committee called the result 'grass without roots'. The Singhvi, Thungon and Gadgil committees urged constitutional recognition. The 64th Amendment Bill passed the Lok Sabha in 1989 but not the Rajya Sabha. The Narasimha Rao Government's 1991 bill became the 73rd Amendment, in force from 24 April 1993.

Part IX covers Articles 243 to 243-O and gives practical shape to Article 40. The Gram Sabha is the foundation and there are three tiers, though a state with up to 20 lakh people may skip the intermediate tier. Compulsory provisions include organising the Gram Sabha, three tiers, direct election of all members, voting rights, a five-year term, a State Election Commission and a State Finance Commission. Voluntary provisions include the manner of electing the village chairperson, backward-class reservation, taxation powers and devolution of the Eleventh Schedule functions. Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram and certain other areas are exempted, and courts cannot interfere in panchayat electoral matters.

SC/ST seats are reserved in proportion to population and women get not less than one-third of seats and chairperson offices. Backward-class reservation is left to the state. The term is five years from the first meeting and elections after dissolution are due within six months. Age 21 suffices for membership. The State Election Commissioner is appointed by the governor but removable only as a high court judge is.

The state legislature may endow panchayats with self-government powers, including plans and schemes on the 29 Eleventh Schedule matters. It may authorise taxes, assign state taxes, give grants-in-aid from the state consolidated fund and create funds. The governor constitutes a State Finance Commission every five years and places its recommendations, with an action taken report, before the state legislature; the legislature of the state may provide for the commission's composition. The Central Finance Commission suggests measures to supplement panchayat resources. Audit is left to the state legislature.

Part IX does not apply to Fifth Schedule areas unless Parliament extends it; PESA (1996) does so for ten states. The Gram Sabha approves plans, and the village panchayat must obtain from it a certification of utilisation of funds. Tribal reservation is not less than one-half of seats and all chairperson seats are reserved for STs; nominations are capped at one-tenth. The Gram Sabha's recommendation is mandatory for minor-mineral licences and leases. Panchayats get ownership of minor forest produce and control over intoxicants, land alienation and money lending.

The Second ARC lists Central Finance Commission grants, State Finance Commission devolution, state loans and grants, scheme allocations and own resources as sources. Gram Panchayats have their own tax domain; the other tiers rely on tolls, fees and non-tax revenue. Reasons for poor performance include inadequate devolution of the 3Fs, bureaucratic control, tied funds, dependence on grants, reluctance to tax, weak Gram Sabhas, parallel bodies and poor infrastructure. Post-1992 committees include Lalit Mathur and Mani Shankar Aiyar.

Article 244 in Part X envisages a special system for 'scheduled areas' and 'tribal areas'. The Fifth Schedule deals with scheduled areas and scheduled tribes in any state except Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram; at present ten states have scheduled areas (Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan). The President may declare a scheduled area, increase or decrease it, alter its boundaries, rescind the designation or make fresh orders, in consultation with the Governor; the criteria (preponderance of tribal population, compactness and reasonable size, a viable administrative entity, economic backwardness compared with neighbouring areas) are not spelt out in the Constitution but are well established. The President must appoint a commission on scheduled areas and scheduled tribes compulsorily after ten years of commencement (Dhebar 1960, report 1961; Bhuria 2002, report 2004). Article 244A concerns an autonomous state in Assam and Article 339 Union control over scheduled areas.

The executive power of a state extends to its scheduled areas; the Governor has a special responsibility and reports to the President annually or whenever required, and the Centre can give directions to the states. Each state with scheduled areas establishes a Tribes Advisory Council of up to 20 members, three-fourths being representatives of the scheduled tribes in the state legislative assembly; the President may direct a similar council in a state with scheduled tribes but no scheduled areas. The Governor may direct that an Act of Parliament or of the state legislature does not apply to a scheduled area or applies with modifications. After consulting the council the Governor may make regulations for peace and good government that prohibit or restrict land transfer by or among scheduled tribe members, regulate land allotment to them and regulate money-lending, and may repeal or amend Acts; all such regulations need the President's assent.

concepts.description: Tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, their constitution as autonomous districts and regions, the councils' composition and the ten tribal areas.
concepts.rule: The Sixth Schedule contains special provisions for the tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, framed to preserve democratic traditions and cultural diversity and conceived as tribal self-rule. The tribal areas are constituted as autonomous districts but do not fall outside the executive authority of the state. The Governor can organise and re-organise the districts (areas, names, boundaries) and divide a district with different tribes into autonomous regions. A district council has 30 members, four nominated by the Governor and the rest elected on adult franchise; elected members hold office for five years unless dissolved earlier and nominated members during the Governor's pleasure; each region has a separate regional council. The Governor may appoint a commission and dissolve a council on its recommendation. The ten tribal areas are: Assam 3, Meghalaya 3, Tripura 1, Mizoram 3.

The district and regional councils administer their areas and make laws on specified matters such as land, forests, canal water, shifting cultivation, village administration, inheritance of property, marriage and divorce and social customs, all with the Governor's assent. They can constitute village councils or courts for suits and cases between the tribes and hear appeals; the Governor specifies the High Court's jurisdiction. The district council can establish, construct or manage primary schools, dispensaries, markets, ferries, fisheries and roads, and make regulations (with the Governor's assent) for the control of money lending and trading by non-tribals. The councils assess and collect land revenue and impose certain specified taxes. Acts of Parliament and of the state legislature do not apply to autonomous areas or apply with modifications; in Assam the Governor directs for both, in Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram the President for Parliament's Acts and the Governor for the state legislature's.

The Fifth Schedule covers scheduled areas and scheduled tribes in all states except the four north-eastern states, which fall under the Sixth Schedule. In the Fifth, the President declares the area, a Tribes Advisory Council advises, the Governor reports to the President and makes regulations needing the President's assent; in the Sixth, the Governor organises autonomous districts, district and regional councils make laws needing the Governor's assent, and the emphasis is on self-rule because many communities had ruled themselves until the British subjugated them in the 19th century. The state's executive power extends to scheduled areas and autonomous districts do not fall outside it. Both systems allow Acts to be made inapplicable or modified. Numbers: ten states with scheduled areas, ten tribal areas, 20 members of the Tribes Advisory Council, 30 members of a district council.

On 13 August 2014 the Government scrapped the 65-year-old Planning Commission and announced a new body; the NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) was established on 1 January 2015 as its successor. Like the Planning Commission it was created by an executive resolution of the Union Cabinet, so it is neither constitutional nor statutory. It is the premier policy think tank of the Government and gives directional and policy inputs and technical advice to the Centre and States. The centre-to-state one-way flow of the Planning Commission era is to give way to a continuing partnership of States, with a collaborative and bottom-up approach in place of command and control. It rests on three foundations: States as equal partners (cooperative federalism), a knowledge hub, and a collaborative platform for implementation.

The Prime Minister is the Chairperson. The Governing Council has the Chief Ministers of all States, the Chief Ministers of Union Territories with legislatures (Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu and Kashmir) and the Lt. Governors of the other Union Territories. Regional Councils are formed for a specified tenure on issues affecting more than one State or region, convened by the Prime Minister and chaired by the Chairperson or a nominee; special invitees are experts nominated by the Prime Minister. The full-time framework has a Vice-Chairperson (Cabinet Minister rank), full-time members (Minister of State rank), a maximum of two part-time members on rotation, a maximum of four ex-officio members from the Union Council of Ministers, a CEO appointed for a fixed tenure in the rank of Secretary, and a secretariat as deemed necessary.

The objectives include a shared vision with States, cooperative federalism, village-level plans aggregated upwards, national security interests on areas referred to it, attention to sections at risk, monitoring with mid-course corrections, partnerships with think tanks, a resource centre and a platform to resolve inter-sectoral issues. Its activities fall into the Team India Hub (federalism and policy frameworks) and the Knowledge and Innovation Hub (resource centre, partnerships); the functions are four heads: policy and programme framework, co-operative and competitive federalism, monitoring and evaluation, and think-tank, knowledge and innovation hub. There are 25 verticals/cells (Annual Report 2022-23). The seven guiding principles are Antyodaya, Inclusion, Village, Demographic dividend, People's Participation, Governance and Sustainability, and there are seven pillars of effective governance.

The NITI Aayog brings States together as 'Team India' on the premise that strong States make a strong nation. Its cooperative-federalism steps include meetings with Chief Ministers, subgroups of Chief Ministers, sharing best practices, the Aspirational Districts Programme, model laws on land leasing and agriculture marketing, and models such as the DSSS and SATH. It promotes competitive federalism through transparent rankings and indices (School Education Quality, State Health, Composite Water Management, SDG, India Innovation) and monthly delta rankings of Aspirational Districts. NILERD (formerly IAMR) is a central autonomous organisation, and the DMEO, set up in 2015 by merging the PEO (1952) and the IEO (2010), is an attached office whose 15 regional offices closed in 2017.

The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950 by an executive resolution of the Union Cabinet on the recommendation of the Advisory Planning Board (1946, K.C. Neogi), so it was neither constitutional nor statutory. Its seven functions covered assessing resources, formulating a plan, setting priorities, indicating retarding factors, deciding machinery, appraising progress and advising on referred matters; it was only a staff agency with no executive responsibility. It was chaired by the Prime Minister, with a Deputy Chairman as de facto executive head, part-time Central Ministers, four to seven full-time experts and a member-secretary; the States were not represented. Critics called it a Super Cabinet, Parallel Cabinet and Fifth Wheel of the Coach, the First ARC and K. Santhanam criticised its role, and P.V. Rajamannar noted an overlap with the Finance Commission.

The National Development Council was established in August 1952 by an executive resolution on the recommendation of the First Five Year Plan (draft outline), and is neither constitutional nor statutory. It consists of the Prime Minister as chairman, all Union Cabinet Ministers (since 1967), the Chief Ministers of all States, the Chief Ministers or administrators of all Union Territories and the members of the Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog). Its objectives are cooperation of States, mobilising national resources, common economic policies and balanced development; its functions include prescribing guidelines for the Plan, considering the Plan prepared by the Planning Commission, assessing resources and reviewing the Plan. Its last (57th) meeting on 27 December 2012 approved the 12th Plan, and on 1 January 2016 it was reported that its powers would pass to the NITI Aayog's Governing Council, though no resolution had been passed.

concepts.description: The fourteen committees and commissions listed, who headed or appointed them, what each studied and when, and the four heads under which the resulting reforms are grouped.
concepts.idea: Fourteen bodies are listed from the 1971-72 Joint Parliamentary Committee to the Law Commission's 255th Report (2015) whose recommendations produced the reforms.
concepts.rule: The list begins with the Joint Parliamentary Committee on Amendments to Election Laws (1971-72) and the unofficial Tarkunde Committee, appointed by Jaya Prakash Narayan in 1974 during his Total Revolution movement, which reported in 1975. The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) was appointed by the V.P. Singh Government when Goswami was Law Minister, and some of its recommendations were implemented in 1996. The Vohra Committee (1993) examined the nexus between crime and politics, and the Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998), appointed by the BJP-led Government and reporting in 1999, upheld state funding of elections. Other entries are the Election Commission's recommendations (1998) and report (2004), the Law Commission's 170th (1999), 244th (2014) and 255th (2015) reports, the Venkatachaliah commission (2000-2002), the Second ARC report headed by Veerappa Moily (2007), the Tankha Core Committee (2010) and the J.S. Verma report on criminal law (2013). The reforms are studied under four heads: before 1996, of 1996, after 1996 and since 2010.
concepts.example: A question that asks which committee dealt with state funding of elections is answered by the Indrajit Gupta Committee, not by the Dinesh Goswami or Vohra committees.

concepts.rule: The 61st Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18, and a 1989 Act placed roll staff on deputation to the Election Commission, set proposers for Rajya Sabha and council polls at 10 per cent of electors or ten, whichever is less, enabled EVMs and provided for adjourning or countermanding polls for booth capturing. The Election Commission decided in 1993 to issue photo identity cards to check bogus voting and impersonation. The 1996 reforms list candidates in three categories in alphabetical order, disqualify for six years those convicted under the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, ban liquor for 48 hours before the close of poll, and require ten proposers for a candidate not sponsored by a recognised party and one for a recognised party's candidate. They also stop countermanding on a candidate's death with a seven-day option for a recognised party (current practice countermands the poll when a recognised party's candidate dies), require by-elections within six months with two exceptions, give a paid holiday on polling day, limit candidates to two constituencies, make arms near polling stations a cognizable offence and cut the campaign gap from 20 to 14 days.
concepts.example: A candidate of a registered-unrecognised party needs ten registered electors as proposers, while a recognised party's candidate needs one.

concepts.rule: In 1997 the proposers and seconders for the President rose from 10 to 50 and for the Vice-President from 5 to 20, and the deposit for both went from Rs 2,500 to Rs 15,000. In 1998 staff of local authorities, nationalised banks, universities, LIC, government undertakings and aided institutions became available for election duty, in 1999 notified classes could vote by postal ballot only, and in 2003 service voters of the Armed Forces could opt for proxy voting. A 2003 Commission order made candidates declare convictions, pending serious cases, assets of self, spouse and dependents, liabilities and education, and false information is an electoral offence. In 2003 the Rajya Sabha domicile requirement was removed and an open ballot, shown to the party's nominated agent, replaced the secret ballot to curb cross-voting and money power; travel of campaigning leaders is exempt from candidate expenses, rolls are supplied free to recognised-party candidates and electronic media time is shared equitably. Braille signage was tried at Asifnagar in 2004, in Delhi in 2008 and used in the 2009 Lok Sabha elections.
concepts.example: A Rajya Sabha elector who belongs to a party must show the marked ballot to the party's nominated agent.

concepts.rule: The Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 2009, effective 1 February 2010, bars conducting and publicising exit polls during the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly elections for the period the Election Commission notifies. It fixed a three-month limit for sending a corrupt practice case to the President, brought all officials appointed or deputed by the Commission within the corrupt practice of obtaining assistance and raised deposits to Rs 25,000 and Rs 12,500 (Lok Sabha) and Rs 10,000 and Rs 5,000 (assembly) for general and SC/ST candidates. Appeals against Electoral Registration Officers now go to the District Magistrate or equivalent and further to the state's Chief Electoral Officer. In 2010 citizens living abroad who have not acquired another citizenship became entitled to register in the constituency of their passport residence, and in 2013 online filing of enrolment applications was provided through the Registration of the Electors (Amendment) Rules, 2013.
concepts.example: An Indian citizen working abroad who has not taken foreign citizenship can be registered in the constituency of the residence mentioned in her passport.

concepts.rule: On the Supreme Court's directions the Commission provided a NOTA option from the 2013 assembly elections, continued in 2014; if NOTA votes exceed those of any candidate the candidate with the most votes is declared elected. The VVPAT is an independent system attached to the EVM; its slip is visible for seven seconds, then falls into a sealed dropbox, the law was amended in 2013, the Court allowed phased introduction as an 'indispensable requirement', and it was first used at Noksen, Nagaland in 2013. In 2013 the Court upheld a Patna High Court order that a person in jail or police custody cannot contest, and Parliament amended the Representation of the People Act, 1951 so that such a person remains an elector and a legislator is disqualified only under the Act. In Lily Thomas v Union of India (2013) the Court struck down Section 8(4) and made disqualification of convicted MPs and MLAs immediate; the Bill to nullify it was withdrawn. For elections after 1 May 2015, ballot papers and EVMs carry the candidate's picture, name and symbol, and a missing photo is no ground to reject nomination.
concepts.example: A voter in an assembly election in 2013 could press NOTA to reject every candidate; the leading candidate would still be declared elected.

concepts.description: The 2003 rules on party contributions, the 2017 cash and corporate donation changes, the electoral bond scheme as notified in 2018, foreign funding, and the Election Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021.
concepts.idea: Party funding rules were being relaxed and re-routed between 2003 and 2018, and the 2021 Act linking rolls with Aadhaar and widening enrolment dates and premises.
concepts.rule: In 2003 parties were allowed to accept any amount from any person or company other than a government company, with contributions above Rs 20,000 reported to the Commission for income tax relief and companies given income tax exemption. The 2017 budget lowered the anonymous cash donation limit from Rs 20,000 to Rs 2,000 and removed the 7.5 per cent of net profit cap on corporate contributions and the duty to report them in the profit and loss account. The Electoral Bond Scheme notified in 2018 was a bearer instrument without the buyer's name, bought by citizens or Indian entities in denominations from Rs 1,000 to Rs 1 crore, usable for donations to registered parties with at least one per cent of votes and encashed through an authorised bank account, with buyer details confidential except to courts or in criminal cases. The 2018 budget allowed foreign funds to parties by amending the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010. The Election Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 enabled Aadhaar linking, specified four qualifying dates, allowed spouses of service voters to vote in person or by post and expanded requisition of premises. The Electoral Bond Scheme and the removal of the corporate-donation cap and of the duty to report such donations were struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2024; the description above is the position as notified before that ruling.
concepts.example: A donor giving a party Rs 5,000 in anonymous cash would exceed the Rs 2,000 limit fixed by the 2017 budget.

concepts.rule: The legislature makes laws that apply to everyone; states have their own legislatures making laws for the state. The executive implements laws and takes policy decisions and has two parts. The political executive are elected leaders: the prime minister, chief ministers and ministers, and the president and governors, whose roles are mostly formal (the Governor is appointed by the President and is not elected). They serve a fixed time, usually five years. The permanent executive are officers selected through exams such as those by the UPSC, called bureaucrats or civil servants, who are not changed after elections and give expert advice, implement policies and manage services. Well-known services include IFS, IAS, IPS, IRS and IFoS. C.B. Muthamma became the first woman to join the Indian Foreign Service in 1949 and won a Supreme Court case against gender bias.

concepts.description: Direct and indirect elections (Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, Councils, President), the duration of the Houses, voting behaviour and psephology.
concepts.example: A President is chosen by an electoral college of elected legislators, while a Lok Sabha member is chosen directly by the voters of a constituency.

concepts.description: First-past-the-post, proportional representation by the single transferable vote, and the bicameral state legislatures.
concepts.example: A candidate with 31 per cent of the votes wins a Lok Sabha seat in a four-cornered contest under first-past-the-post.

concepts.description: The Representation of the People Acts of 1950 and 1951, the Delimitation Acts, constitutional bars on courts, and related rules and orders.
concepts.rule: The 1950 Act allocates seats and provides for registration of electors; the 1951 Act covers conduct of elections, qualifications and disqualifications, corrupt practices and election petitions. Delimitation is by Parliament's law under Articles 82 and 170, frozen at the 1971 level by the 42nd Amendment and extended up to 2026 by the 84th (Article 82 itself refers to the first census after 2026); the Delimitation Act 2002 used the 2001 census. The validity of delimitation laws cannot be questioned in any court, and election petitions go to the High Courts.
concepts.example: A candidate challenging a Lok Sabha result files an election petition in the High Court, with appeal to the Supreme Court.

concepts.description: The constitutional status, composition, independence, powers and election machinery of the Election Commission.
concepts.example: The Commission announces the schedule, the Model Code of Conduct takes effect at once and observers monitor the poll and the expenditure.

concepts.description: Party systems, recognition of national and state parties, the Tenth Schedule, coalitions and regional parties.
concepts.example: A legislator who votes against the party whip, without permission and uncondoned within 15 days, faces disqualification decided by the presiding officer.

concepts.description: Defection and the Tenth Schedule's rules and reasons, the determinants of voting behaviour, coalition governments and the role of regional and national parties as challenges to free and fair elections.
concepts.example: A coalition of partners with different programmes falls when a partner withdraws, a recognised demerit of coalitions.
